body:
When we look at a set of numbers, a box plot helps us see where the middle values lie and which points sit far away from the rest.

For our numbers 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12, and 40, the median is 8, the lower quartile is 5.5, and the upper quartile is 10.5.

To find outliers, we calculate the interquartile range, which is the span between the upper and lower quartiles, giving $10.5 - 5.5 = 5$.

```rh-diagram

```

Fences mark the boundary where normal values end and unusual points begin. We multiply this range by $1.5$ to get $7.5$, then subtract it from the lower quartile and add it to the upper quartile.

This puts the lower fence at $-2$ and the upper fence at $18$.

title: Finding Outliers with the 1.5 IQR Rule
body:
When looking at response times like 80 to 300 milliseconds, some values are way higher than the rest. The interquartile range, or IQR, measures the span of the middle half of these response times.

Subtracting the lower quartile from the upper quartile gives us this spread.

Look at the box plot below to see how the middle values bunch up while the extreme value sits far apart.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Response times with outlier","caption":"IQR is 14 ms. The upper fence is 125 ms, making 300 ms an outlier.","kind":"box-plot","x":{"label":"Response time (ms)","min":70,"max":310,"unit":"ms"},"boxes":[{"label":"Response times","whiskerLow":80,"q1":87.5,"median":95,"q3":101.5,"whiskerHigh":110,"fences":{"lower":66.5,"upper":122.5},"outliers":[{"label":"Extreme value","value":300}]}]}}
```

The 1.5 times IQR rule takes that middle spread and stretches it outward to set a boundary called a fence. Any data point sitting beyond this fence is marked as an outlier rather than stretching the main whiskers.

title: Finding Outliers with the 1.5 x IQR Rule
body:
When you have a set of response times like a list of server delays, some values might be extreme. The interquartile range measures the spread of the middle half of your data.

Look at the box plot to see how fences isolate unusual points.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Response times with fence and outlier","caption":"The IQR is 15. The upper fence is 125, making 300 an outlier.","kind":"box-plot","x":{"label":"Time (ms)","min":70,"max":320,"unit":"ms"},"boxes":[{"label":"Response times","whiskerLow":80,"q1":87.5,"median":95,"q3":102.5,"whiskerHigh":110,"fences":{"lower":65,"upper":125},"outliers":[{"label":"Outlier","value":300}]}]}}
```

The rule multiplies this middle spread by 1.5 to set outer fences. Any data point sitting beyond these fences is marked separately as an outlier.

In our times, the middle values give an IQR of 15. The upper fence lands at 125, leaving 300 as a clear outlier.

body:
Imagine measuring how long a web page takes to load. The recorded times are shown as a list of data points.

The box‑plot below displays the five‑number summary derived from those points and the fences that the 1.5 × IQR rule creates.

```rh-diagram

```
